Section P.3 gives a random variable a **probability function** $p(x)$ — every
value gets a probability between 0 and 1, and the probabilities **sum to 1** —
from which the **mean** (expected value) and **standard deviation** follow by
exactly weighted averaging,
$$\mu=\sum x\cdot p(x)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma^2=\sum(x-\mu)^2\cdot p(x).$$
Section P.4 shortcuts one whole family of discrete random variables: when $n$
trials are **fixed in advance**, **independent**, and each has the **same
probability of success** $p$, the count of successes is **binomial** with
$$P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k},\qquad \mu=np,\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{np(1-p)}.$$
Section P.5 turns to **continuous** random variables, whose probabilities are
**areas under a density curve** — total area 1 — and develops the most
important density of all, the **normal curve** $N(\mu,\sigma)$: bell-shaped,
centered at $\mu$, with 95% of the area within $\mu\pm2\sigma$. Any normal
question becomes a standard-normal question through the z-score
$z=(x-\mu)/\sigma$, and percentiles go back the other way via
$x=\mu+z\,\sigma$. Below we compute every probability-function statistic
exactly, every binomial probability with `scipy.stats.binom` (cross-checking
the applied exercises with **100000-rep simulations, seed 2026**), and every
normal area/endpoint with `scipy.stats.norm.cdf/ppf`, shading the relevant
regions on density-curve figures throughout. The exercises are from
*Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data* (Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 760–782): the
P.3 applied set works household sizes, fruit-fly lifetimes, used-car sales,
life insurance, ISP pricing, Benford's law, and a board-game die; the P.4
set runs from factorials to airline overbooking; and the P.5 set moves from
standard-normal areas to SAT scores, growth charts, GPA quartiles, bootstrap
means, and grade curving. Every exercise here is computation-from-description, so no datasets
are needed.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

BLUE, RED, ORANGE = "#4c72b0", "#c44e52", "#dd8452"

def pfun(values, probs, solve_at=None):
    """Probability function as a Series; `solve_at` solves the missing '?' entry."""
    p = list(probs)
    if solve_at is not None:
        p[solve_at] = 1 - sum(v for i, v in enumerate(p) if i != solve_at)
    return pd.Series(p, index=list(values), name="p(x)").round(6)

def disc_stats(values, probs):
    """Exact mean, variance and standard deviation of a discrete random variable."""
    x = np.asarray(values, float); p = np.asarray(probs, float)
    mu = float((x * p).sum())
    var = float(((x - mu) ** 2 * p).sum())
    return pd.Series({"Mean": mu, "Variance": var,
                      "Std. dev.": round(float(np.sqrt(var)), 4)})

def pmf_bar(s, highlight=None, xlabel="x", figsize=(5, 2.5), title=None):
    """Bar plot of a probability function; optionally highlight one value."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    colors = [RED if highlight is not None and v == highlight else BLUE
              for v in s.index]
    ax.bar([str(v) for v in s.index], s.values, color=colors)
    ax.set_ylabel("p(x)"); ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

def binom_tab(n, p):
    """Full binomial probability function for k = 0..n."""
    ks = np.arange(n + 1)
    return pd.DataFrame({"p(k)": np.round(stats.binom.pmf(ks, n, p), 6)},
                        index=ks, columns=["p(k)"]).rename_axis("k")

def binom_sim(n, p, event, reps=100000, seed=2026):
    """Fraction of `reps` simulated B(n, p) counts satisfying `event`."""
    sims = np.random.default_rng(seed).binomial(n, p, reps)
    return float(event(sims).mean())

def _shade_axis(ax, mu, sigma, a, b):
    """Draw N(mu, sigma) on ax with the region between a and b shaded
    (None = open tail); return the shaded area."""
    lo, hi = mu - 4.3 * sigma, mu + 4.3 * sigma
    pts = [v for v in (a, b) if v is not None]
    if pts:
        lo = min(lo, min(pts) - 0.8 * sigma)
        hi = max(hi, max(pts) + 0.8 * sigma)
    x = np.linspace(lo, hi, 900)
    y = stats.norm.pdf(x, mu, sigma)
    ax.plot(x, y, color=BLUE, lw=2)
    aa = lo if a is None else a
    bb = hi if b is None else b
    m = (x >= aa) & (x <= bb)
    ax.fill_between(x[m], y[m], color=RED, alpha=0.6)
    for v in pts:
        ax.axvline(v, color="black", lw=1)
    return float(stats.norm.cdf(b if b is not None else np.inf, mu, sigma)
                 - stats.norm.cdf(a if a is not None else -np.inf, mu, sigma))

def norm_shade(mu, sigma, a=None, b=None, figsize=(6, 2.3), xlabel=None,
               title=None):
    """Single normal density with the region between a and b shaded."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    area = _shade_axis(ax, mu, sigma, a, b)
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel if xlabel else
                  (f"x   N({mu:g}, {sigma:g})" if mu else "z   N(0, 1)"))
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    return area

def norm_pair(mu, sigma, a=None, b=None, xlab=None, figsize=(7.5, 2.6)):
    """Interval (a, b) on N(mu, sigma) beside the matching standardized
    region on N(0, 1), as the conversion exercises request."""
    za = None if a is None else (a - mu) / sigma
    zb = None if b is None else (b - mu) / sigma
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=figsize)
    area = _shade_axis(axes[0], mu, sigma, a, b)
    _shade_axis(axes[1], 0, 1, za, zb)
    axes[0].set_xlabel(xlab if xlab else f"x   N({mu:g}, {sigma:g})")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("z   N(0, 1)")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    return area

def norm_row(mu, sigma, regions, titles, figsize=(10.5, 2.4)):
    """Several shaded regions of the same normal curve, side by side."""
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(regions), figsize=figsize)
    areas = []
    for ax, (a, b), t in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), regions, titles):
        areas.append(_shade_axis(ax, mu, sigma, a, b))
        ax.set_title(t, fontsize=9)
        ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    return areas

def p13_density(x):
    """Reproduction of Figure P.13: small bump near 15, main peak near 24.5."""
    return 0.22 * stats.norm.pdf(x, 15, 2.1) + 0.78 * stats.norm.pdf(x, 24.5, 3.0)

def p13_shade(a=None, b=None, figsize=(6.5, 2.4)):
    """Figure P.13 with the region between a and b shaded; returns its area."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    x = np.linspace(4, 36, 1200)
    y = p13_density(x)
    ax.plot(x, y, color=BLUE, lw=2)
    m = np.ones_like(x, dtype=bool)
    if a is not None:
        m &= x >= a
    if b is not None:
        m &= x <= b
    ax.fill_between(x[m], y[m], color=RED, alpha=0.6)
    for v in (a, b):
        if v is not None:
            ax.axvline(v, color="black", lw=1)
    ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    return float(np.trapezoid(y[m], x[m]))
```

## Exercise P.63

*(Skill Builder 1)* Draw 10 cards from a deck and count the number of hearts.

**Discrete** — the number of hearts is a **count** out of the 10 cards
(possible values 0, 1, …, 10).

## Exercise P.64

*(Skill Builder 1)* Draw 10 cards from a deck and find the proportion that
are hearts.

**Discrete** — the proportion is a count divided by 10, so it can only take
the 11 values 0, 0.1, 0.2, …, 1.

## Exercise P.68

*(Skill Builder 2)* Table P.10 gives a probability function for a random
variable $X$ taking the values 1–4. Verify that it meets the conditions for
being a probability function.

```{python}
#| echo: false
t10 = pfun([1, 2, 3, 4], [0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1])
t10.to_string()
```

Every $p(x)$ is between 0 and 1, and the probabilities **sum to exactly 1**
($0.4+0.3+0.2+0.1=1.0$) — both conditions hold, so Table P.10 is a valid
probability function.

**Not possible.** The given probabilities already sum to $0.5+0.6=1.1>1$,

## Exercise P.78

*(Skill Builder 4)* Mean and standard deviation for the probability function
$x=1,2,3$ with $p(x)=0.2,0.3,0.5$:

```{python}
#| echo: false
disc_stats([1, 2, 3], [0.2, 0.3, 0.5]).to_string()
```

- **(a)** $\mu=\sum x\,p(x)=1(0.2)+2(0.3)+3(0.5)=$ **2.3**.
- **(b)** $\sigma^2=\sum(x-\mu)^2p(x)=0.61$, so $\sigma=$ **0.781**.

## Exercise P.82

**Owner-Occupied Household Size.** Table P.11 gives the probability function
for the household size of an owner-occupied US housing unit:
$p(x)=0.217, 0.363, 0.165, 0.145, 0.067, 0.026, 0.018$ for $x=1,\dots,7$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pown = np.array([0.217, 0.363, 0.165, 0.145, 0.067, 0.026, 0.018])
hs_own = pfun(range(1, 8), pown)
hs_own.to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Probability function for owner-occupied household size, with a 100000-rep simulation (seed 2026) of parts (b)-(d) for comparison"
sim_own = np.random.default_rng(2026).choice(np.arange(1, 8), 100000,
                                             p=pown / pown.sum())
print(pd.DataFrame({"Exact": [round(pown[0] + pown[1], 3),
                              round(pown[4:].sum(), 3),
                              round(1 - pown[0], 3)],
                    "Simulated": [round((sim_own <= 2).mean(), 4),
                                  round((sim_own >= 5).mean(), 4),
                                  round((sim_own > 1).mean(), 4)]},
                   index=["(b) P(X <= 2)", "(c) P(X >= 5)",
                          "(d) P(X > 1)"]).to_string())
pmf_bar(hs_own, xlabel="Household size")
```

- **(a)** The probabilities sum to $0.217+0.363+\cdots+0.018=$ **1.001** —
  equal to 1 up to round-off error in the published table (the simulation
  normalizes to exactly 1).
- **(b)** $P(X\le2)=0.217+0.363=$ **0.580** (simulation: 0.5814).
- **(c)** $P(X\ge5)=0.067+0.026+0.018=$ **0.111** (simulation: 0.1108).
- **(d)** $P(X>1)=1-p(1)=1-0.217=$ **0.783** (simulation: 0.7804) — most
  owner-occupied units house more than one person.

## Exercise P.83

**Renter-Occupied Household Size.** Table P.12 gives the probability function
for the household size of a renter-occupied US housing unit:
$p(x)=0.362, 0.261, 0.153, 0.114, 0.061, 0.027, 0.022$ for $x=1,\dots,7$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
prent = np.array([0.362, 0.261, 0.153, 0.114, 0.061, 0.027, 0.022])

hs_rent.to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false

                                              p=prent / prent.sum())
print(pd.DataFrame({"Exact": [round(prent[0] + prent[1], 3),
                              round(prent[4:].sum(), 3),

                    "Simulated": [round((sim_rent <= 2).mean(), 4),
                                  round((sim_rent >= 5).mean(), 4),
```

- **(a)** The probabilities sum to $0.362+0.261+\cdots+0.022=$ **1.000**.

  the book's answer key.
- **(c)** $P(X\ge5)=0.061+0.027+0.022=$ **0.110** (simulation: 0.1099).
- **(d)** $P(X>1)=1-p(1)=1-0.362=$ **0.638** (simulation: 0.6354).

## Exercise P.84

**Average Household Size for Owner-Occupied Units.** Using Table P.11 in
Exercise P.82 ($p(x)=0.217, 0.363, 0.165, 0.145, 0.067, 0.026, 0.018$ for

```{python}
#| echo: false
pown = np.array([0.217, 0.363, 0.165, 0.145, 0.067, 0.026, 0.018])

                                           p=pown / pown.sum())

           "(b) Std. dev.": round(st_own["Std. dev."], 3),

```

- **(a)** $\mu=\sum x\,p(x)=1(0.217)+2(0.363)+\cdots+7(0.018)=$ **2.635
  people** (simulation: 2.625).

## Exercise P.86

**Fruit Fly Lifetimes.** The probability function in Table P.13 gives possible
lifetimes (in months after emergence) for fruit flies, with one entry missing:
$p(1)=0.30$, $p(2)=?$, $p(3)=0.20$, $p(4)=0.15$, $p(5)=0.10$, $p(6)=0.05$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
fly = pfun([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], [0.30, None, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05], solve_at=1)
fly.to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Fruit-fly lifetime probability function, second-month bar highlighted
pmf_bar(fly, highlight=2, xlabel="Lifetime (months)")
disc_stats(fly.index, fly.values).to_string()
```

- **(a)** The probabilities must sum to 1, so
  $p(2)=1-(0.30+0.20+0.15+0.10+0.05)=$ **0.20** — **20% of fruit flies die in
  their second month**.
- **(b)** $P(X>4)=p(5)+p(6)=0.10+0.05=$ **0.15**.
- **(c)** $\mu=\sum x\,p(x)=1(0.30)+2(0.20)+\cdots+6(0.05)=$ **2.7 months**.
- **(d)** $\sigma^2=\sum(x-\mu)^2p(x)=2.31$, so $\sigma=$ **1.52 months**.

- **(d)** $\sigma^2=\sum(x-\mu)^2p(x)=1.3931$, so $\sigma=$ **1.180 cars**.

## Exercise P.88

**More Fruit Fly Lifetimes.** Using Table P.13 ($p$: 0.30, 0.20, 0.20, 0.15,
0.10, 0.05 for $x=1,\dots,6$):

- **(a)** "Died before the end of its second month" means $X\le2$, which has
  probability $0.30+0.20=0.50$. So
  $$P(X=1\mid X\le2)=\frac{p(1)}{p(1)+p(2)}=\frac{0.30}{0.50}=$$ **0.60**.
- **(b)** "Makes it past its second month" means $X>2$ (probability
  $0.20+0.15+0.10+0.05=0.50$), so
  $$P(X>4\mid X>2)=\frac{p(5)+p(6)}{P(X>2)}=\frac{0.15}{0.50}=$$ **0.30**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
```

## Exercise P.90

**Stephen Curry's Free Throws.** Curry made 90.8% of free throws in 2015–16;
assume each attempt is an independent success with $p=0.908$. Let $X$ be the
number made in **two** attempts, so $X\sim B(2,\ 0.908)$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
curry2 = binom_tab(2, 0.908)
curry2.to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Probability function for free throws made in two attempts
pmf_bar(pd.Series(curry2["p(k)"]), xlabel="Free throws made (of 2)")
```

- **(a)** The probability function is binomial, $B(2, 0.908)$:
  $p(0)=(0.092)^2=$ **0.0085**, $p(1)=2(0.908)(0.092)=$ **0.1671**, and
  $p(2)=(0.908)^2=$ **0.8245**.
- **(b)** $\mu=np=2(0.908)=$ **1.816** free throws.

## Exercise P.91

**Life Insurance.** A non-profit sells five-year contracts to women on their
60th birthday: yearly fee $c$, and a $\$100{,}000$ payment to the family if
the holder dies within the five years (fees then stop). Death probabilities
for ages 60–64: 0.00648, 0.00700, 0.00760, 0.00829, 0.00908.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pdeath = [0.00648, 0.00700, 0.00760, 0.00829, 0.00908]
psurv = 1 - sum(pdeath)
ins = pd.DataFrame({
    "Outcome": [f"Dies at {a}" for a in range(60, 65)] + ["Survives 5 years"],
    "Profit X": [f"{k+1}c - 100000" for k in range(5)] + ["5c"],
    "Probability": pdeath + [round(psurv, 5)]})
ins.to_string(index=False)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
fees = np.arange(1, 6)
emu = sum((k + 1) * p for k, p in enumerate(pdeath)) + 5 * psurv
c_be = 100000 * sum(pdeath) / emu
pd.Series({"Expected fees collected": round(emu, 5),
           "Expected payout": 100000 * sum(pdeath),
           "(b) Mean of X": f"{emu:.4f}c - {100000 * sum(pdeath):.0f}",
           "(c) Break-even fee c": round(c_be, 2)}).to_string()
```

- **(a)** A holder who dies at age $60+k$ has paid $k+1$ yearly fees (fees are
  paid at the start of each year) before the $\$100{,}000$ payout, so $X$
  takes values $(k+1)c-100{,}000$ with the death probabilities, and $5c$ with
  probability $1-0.03845=0.96155$ (table above).
- **(b)** Expected fees are
  $c\,[5(0.96155)+1(0.00648)+2(0.00700)+3(0.00760)+4(0.00829)+5(0.00908)] =
  4.9296\,c$, and the expected payout is $100{,}000(0.03845)=\$3845$, so
  $$\mu= \textbf{4.9296}\,c - \textbf{3845}\ \text{dollars}.$$
- **(c)** Break-even means $\mu=0$: $c=3845/4.9296\approx$ **\$779.98 per
  year**.

**Internet Pricing.** An ISP sells Ultra at $\$39.95$, Premium at $\$29.95$
(twice as many customers), and Basic at $\$23.95$ (three times as many). So
the customer mix is $1:2:3$ and $P(\text{Ultra})=1/6$,
$P(\text{Premium})=2/6$, $P(\text{Basic})=3/6$.

```{python}

                  39.95: "Ultra $39.95"}).to_string()
```


- **(a)** The probability function is $P(X=23.95)=0.5$, $P(X=29.95)=1/3$,

  per month — the average revenue per customer.
- **(c)** $\sigma^2=\sum(x-\mu)^2p(x)\approx32.89$, so $\sigma\approx$
  **\$5.73**.

## Exercise P.94

**Getting to the Finish.** A player rolls a fair die until the exact needed
value appears; the number of turns $X$ has the geometric probability function
$P(X=k)=p(1-p)^{k-1}$ with $p=1/6$.

- **(a)** Finishing on the third turn:
  $$P(X=3)=\frac16\Bigl(\frac56\Bigr)^{2}=\frac{25}{216}\approx$$ **0.1157**.
- **(b)** Taking **more than** three turns means the first three rolls all
  fail: $$P(X>3)=\Bigl(\frac56\Bigr)^{3}=\frac{125}{216}\approx$$ **0.5787**.

## Exercise P.128

**Mean and Standard Deviation of a Proportion.** If $X\sim B(n, p)$ counts
successes, the sample proportion is $\hat p=X/n$.

**Mean:** linearity of expectation gives
$$\mu_{\hat p}=E\!\left[\frac{X}{n}\right]=\frac{1}{n}E[X]=\frac{np}{n}=p.$$

**Standard deviation:** constants pull out of a square root as their absolute
value, so
$$\sigma_{\hat p}=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{X}{n}\right)}
=\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{np(1-p)}=\sqrt{\frac{np(1-p)}{n^2}}
=\boxed{\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}}.$$

So a proportion is centered at the true $p$ with standard error
$\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ — the same formulas used for inference on a proportion
later in the book.

```{python}
xb = np.linspace(0, 7, 500)
ax.plot(xb, 0.54 * stats.norm.pdf(xb, 0.9, 0.75)
        + 0.46 * stats.norm.pdf(xb, 3.2, 1.2), color=BLUE, lw=2)
xc = np.linspace(7.3, 13.9, 400)
ax.plot(xc, 3.6 * stats.norm.pdf(xc, 10.6, 0.9), color=BLUE, lw=2)
ax.text(-1.2, 1.53, "(a)", ha="center", fontsize=10)
ax.text(2.2, 0.42, "(b)", ha="center", fontsize=10)
ax.text(10.6, 1.63, "(c)", ha="center", fontsize=10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.75)
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Curve (c) is not a density curve.** A density must have **total area 1**,
but (c) is both tall (peak ≈ 1.6) *and* wide (spanning roughly 6 units, from
about 7.5 to 13.5); its area is roughly $1.6\times6\times0.5\approx 4\text{–}5$,
far more than 1. By contrast, curve (a) is tall but very narrow (a peak of
1.5 can only span about 2 units and still enclose area 1), and the low,
bumpy curve (b) averages just the right height (~0.2 over 5 units) to enclose
area 1 — both are legitimate densities.

## Exercise P.149

*(Skill Builder 7)* Convert the **area below 40** for a $N(48, 5)$
distribution to an equivalent area on the standard normal curve.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: P.149 — area below 40 on N(48, 5) equals the area below z = -1.6 on N(0, 1)
a149 = norm_pair(48, 5, None, 40, xlab="x   N(48, 5)")
pd.Series({"Endpoint x": 40, "z-score": (40 - 48) / 5,
           "Area (both curves)": round(a149, 4)}).to_string()
```

$$z=\frac{40-48}{5}=\textbf{-1.6}$$ The area below 40 on $N(48,5)$ — about
**0.0548** — is exactly the area below $z=-1.6$ on $N(0,1)$: the two shaded
regions above have identical area, only the horizontal scale differs.


The middle 80% of a standard normal runs from the 10th to the 90th
percentile, $z=\pm$ **1.28**. On the $N(100,15)$ scale that is
$100\pm1.28(15)$, i.e. from about **80.8 to 119.2**.

## Exercise P.168

**Curving Grades on an Exam.** The exam was designed for $N(75, 10)$ but
came out $N(62, 18)$. The curve standardizes each score with the $N(62,18)$
scale, then un-standardizes onto the $N(75,10)$ scale: new $=75+z\cdot10$
with $z=(\text{old}-62)/18$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: P.168 — original scores 47 and 90 on N(62, 18) map to 66.7 and 90.6 on N(75, 10)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 2.6))
for ax, (m, s, pts, lab) in zip(axes, [
        (62, 18, [47, 90], "Original   N(62, 18)"),
        (75, 10, [66.67, 90.56], "Curved   N(75, 10)")]):
    x = np.linspace(m - 4.2 * s, m + 4.2 * s, 800)
    ax.plot(x, stats.norm.pdf(x, m, s), color=BLUE, lw=2)
    for p_ in pts:
        ax.axvline(p_, color=RED, lw=1.5)
        ax.text(p_, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.02, f" {p_:g}", color=RED, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel(lab)
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
rows = []
for s_ in (47, 90):
    z = (s_ - 62) / 18
    rows.append({"Original score": s_, "z-score": round(z, 4),
                 "Curved score = 75 + 10z": round(75 + z * 10, 2)})
pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False)
```

- Score **47**: $z=(47-62)/18=-0.833$, so the curved grade is
  $75-0.833(10)\approx$ **66.7**.
- Score **90**: $z=(90-62)/18=1.556$, so the curved grade is
  $75+1.556(10)\approx$ **90.6**.

The student hurt by the fire alarm gains roughly 20 points; the student who
finished comfortably stays about the same — the curve preserves each
student's *relative standing* (percentile) while restoring the intended
center and spread.

## Exercise P.169

**Empirical Rule for Normal Distributions.** Pick any positive $\mu$ and
$\sigma$ — we use $N(100,\ 15)$ — and verify the empirical rule.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: P.169 — areas within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean for N(100, 15)
mu, sigma = 100, 15
areas169 = norm_row(mu, sigma,
                    [(mu - sigma, mu + sigma), (mu - 2 * sigma, mu + 2 * sigma),
                     (mu - 3 * sigma, mu + 3 * sigma)],
                    ["within 1 sd", "within 2 sd", "within 3 sd"])
pd.Series({"(a) within 2 sd": round(areas169[1], 3),
           "(b) within 1 sd": round(areas169[0], 3),
           "(c) within 3 sd": round(areas169[2], 3)}).to_string()
```

For $N(100,\ 15)$ (any values work):

- **(a)** $P(70<X<130)=P(-2<Z<2)\approx$ **0.954** — about 95% of values fall
  within two standard deviations of the mean. ✓
- **(b)** $P(85<X<115)=P(-1<Z<1)\approx$ **0.683** — about 68% within one
  standard deviation.
- **(c)** $P(55<X<145)=P(-3<Z<3)\approx$ **0.997** — about 99.7% within
  three standard deviations.
- **(d)** **Yes — the answers are the same for every normal distribution.**
  If $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma)$ then $Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma\sim N(0,1)$ regardless of
  the particular $\mu$ and $\sigma$, so every normal probability is just a
  standard-normal area in disguise: the intervals $\mu\pm\sigma$,
  $\mu\pm2\sigma$, $\mu\pm3\sigma$ always capture the same 68%/95%/99.7%
  (the **empirical rule**).

:::
